narrative.text: Chapter 1 Introduction motivating the algorithmic study of decision-making problems that require deciding between sticking with an option and giving up when investment is needed to realize payoffs. Traces the progression of the thesis from general abstract sequential decision-making models to distributional settings and concrete theoretical models of social phenomena.

Section 1.1 ('Unifying Framework') contrasting two theoretical perspectives on decision-making: the classical sequential decision-making perspective (fixing the setting and environment while designing the agent policy) and the social modeling perspective (fixing the setting and agent decision rule while intervening on the environment, akin to mechanism design).

Section 1.2 ('Outline of Thesis') summarizing the two-part structure of the dissertation: Part I on sequential decision-making in the improving multi-armed bandits (IMAB) problem, and Part II on theoretical models in social epistemology for ambitious decision-making and reflection on the epistemic value of abstraction.

Section 1.2.1 ('Part I: Improving Multi-Armed Bandits') outlining Chapters 2–4: formalizing the IMAB problem with diminishing returns (Chapter 2), proving nearly matching O(sqrt(k) log k) upper and Omega(sqrt(k)) lower approximation bounds in the worst case (Chapter 3), and developing data-driven algorithm design and sample complexity bounds over distributions of IMAB instances (Chapter 4).

Section 1.2.2 ('Part II: Social Epistemology') outlining Chapters 5–7: examining three epistemic roles of mathematical models in studying social phenomena (Chapter 5), formalizing Morton's pessimism traps via information cascades and designing subsidy interventions (Chapter 6), and modeling the interplay of grit and financial support as a specialized IMAB instance (Chapter 7).

Section 1.2.3 ('Bibliographic Notes') listing the four conference papers and collaborations underlying the thesis: Chapters 2–3 from [BR25] (ALT 2025, with Avrim Blum), Chapter 4 from [BGRS26] (UAI 2026, with Avrim Blum, Marten Garicano, and Dravyansh Sharma), Chapter 5 newly written, Chapter 6 from [BDRT25] (FORC 2025), and Chapter 7 from [BDRT26] (AAAI 2026, with Avrim Blum, Emily Diana, and Alexander Williams Tolbert).

Section 1.3 ('Takeaways') summarizing the three primary contributions of the dissertation: worst-case and data-driven algorithmic guarantees for improving multi-armed bandits, mathematical formalisms and interventions for pessimism traps and grit in social epistemology, and methodological guidelines for applying theoretical computer science models to social phenomena.
Heading-only block containing the section number '2.1' under 'Setting and Preliminaries' at the start of Chapter 2, with the prose body following in the next block.

Section 2.1 ('Improving Multi-Armed Bandit Setting') introducing the improving multi-armed bandits (IMAB) problem in which pulling an arm yields rewards that increase with the number of pulls of that arm, motivating it via technology R&D investment and hyperparameter tuning, and contrasting worst-case analysis with data-driven distributional analysis.

Section 2.2 ('Formal Preliminaries') and Definition 2.2.1 formally defining an improving multi-armed bandits instance I as a collection of k arms, each with an unknown nondecreasing reward function f_i(t_i) of the number of pulls t_i of arm i.

Section 2.2.1 ('External and Policy Regret, Adversary Model') defining the oblivious adversary model and comparing external regret against policy regret in non-stationary stateful bandits, illustrating with a two-arm example why policy regret (competing against the optimal policy in hindsight) is the appropriate stronger comparator for IMAB.

Section 2.2.2 ('Optimality and Competitive Ratio') observing that the optimal policy in hindsight pulls the single arm i* maximizing cumulative reward for all T steps, defining the expected competitive ratio (Definition 2.2.2), and showing why non-trivial high-probability competitive guarantees are impossible in this setting.

Section 2.2.3 ('Diminishing Returns') explaining why arbitrary increasing reward functions prevent any meaningful guarantee and stating Definition 2.2.3, which restricts each arm's reward function f to satisfy diminishing returns (discrete concavity: f(t+1) - f(t) <= f(t) - f(t-1)) with f(0) = 0.

Section 2.3 ('Related Work') reviewing prior literature on improving/rising bandits ([HKR16], [PNGK23], [MTPR22], [MMT+24]), bandits with switching costs, rotting/restless bandits, and best-arm identification, accompanied by Table 2.1 summarizing regret and competitive ratio results for IMAB.

Section 3.1 ('Worst-Case Setting') framing the Chapter 3 improving multi-armed bandits problem as a minimax game against an oblivious adversary who knows the randomized algorithm and selects the worst-case instance I to minimize the algorithm's expected performance.

Section 3.1.1 ('Lower Bound') briefly stating the main worst-case results of Chapter 3: randomized algorithms achieve an O(sqrt(k)) approximation ratio when the best arm's maximum value is known and O(sqrt(k) log k) when unknown, matching an Omega(sqrt(k)) lower bound.

Sections 3.1.2–3.3 ('Upper Bound' and 'Lower Bound') proving Theorem 3.2.1 and Corollary 3.2.1 via Yao's principle that no randomized algorithm can beat an Omega(sqrt(k)) approximation factor on increasing bandits, and presenting Algorithm 1 (thresholded round-robin over a randomly permuted arm order when m ~ f*(T) is known) with its O(sqrt(k)) competitive ratio proof.

Section 3.4 ('Removing Assumptions') introducing Algorithm 2, which removes the assumption that the best arm's final value f*(T) is known by pulling each arm T/(2k) times (for T > 4k) to bound f*(T) within [L, U] and sampling an estimate L * 2^j from a logarithmic grid.

Section 3.4.1 ('Computing Range for a Fixed Arm') and Lemma 3.4.1 proving that pulling a single arm T/(2k) times under diminishing returns yields lower and upper bounds [m_hat_L, m_hat_U] on f(T) satisfying m_hat_U <= 2k * m_hat_L.

Section 3.4.2 ('Upper and Lower Bounds on Final Value of Best Arm From Exploration') and Lemma 3.4.2 combining the per-arm exploration ranges to construct a global interval [L, U] containing f*(T) with ratio U/L <= 4k.

Section 3.4.3 ('Reward Approximation Guarantee With Learned Parameter') and Theorem 3.4.3 proving that sampling the guessed threshold m uniformly from the logarithmic grid over [L, U] in Algorithm 2 and running Algorithm 1 on the remaining horizon achieves an O(sqrt(k) log k) competitive ratio.

Section 3.4.4 ('Removing Dependence on Having To Know T') presenting Algorithm 3 and Lemma 3.4.4, which apply a doubling trick starting from T_0 = 4k to achieve an O(sqrt(k) log k) competitive ratio without prior knowledge of the time horizon T.

Section 3.5 ('Conclusion') summarizing Chapter 3's nearly tight Omega(sqrt(k)) lower and O(sqrt(k) log k) upper bounds for worst-case IMAB and transitioning to Chapter 4's beyond-worst-case data-driven algorithm design setting.

Section 4.1 ('Data-Driven Algorithm Design Setting') introducing the distributional setting for Chapter 4 where instances are drawn from an unknown distribution D and historical samples are used to select near-optimal algorithm parameters for cumulative reward maximization and best-arm identification.

Section 4.1.1 ('Our Contributions') enumerating Chapter 4's four main results: defining a concavity strength parameter beta with optimal O(k^{beta/(1+beta)}) competitive ratio via the PTRR_alpha family, bounding the sample complexity of learning alpha from data, designing the Hybrid_{alpha,B} family for best-of-both-worlds best-arm identification, and bounding its two-parameter sample complexity.

Section 4.2 ('Data-Driven Algorithm Design Perspective') motivating hyperparameter transfer across training tasks and formally defining the Hyperparameter Transfer Setting (Definition 4.2.2) and sample complexity N(epsilon, delta) for learning parameters over an algorithm family.

Section 4.3 ('Using Strength of Concavity') motivating a parameterized family of IMAB algorithms that includes the worst-case optimal algorithm of [BR25] while achieving improved approximation guarantees on instances with stronger concavity.

Section 4.3.1 ('Algorithm Family') and Definition 4.3.1 defining the alpha-Power-Thresholded Round Robin family PTRR = {PTRR_alpha : alpha in (0, 1]} (Algorithm 4), which pulls each randomly ordered arm i while f_i(t_i) >= m * (t_i / tau)^alpha.

Section 4.3.2 ('Sharper Competitive Ratio') defining the Concavity Envelope Exponent beta_I of an instance and proving that PTRR_alpha achieves an O(k^gamma) competitive ratio where gamma = max{alpha/(1+alpha), beta_I - alpha(1 - beta_I)}, yielding the optimal O(k^{beta/(1+beta)}) bound when alpha = beta alongside a matching lower bound.

Section 4.3.3 ('Sample Complexity of Learning the Curvature Parameter') proving that the dual loss of PTRR_alpha is piecewise monotonic with at most kT discontinuities per permutation, bounding its pseudo-dimension by O(log(kT)), and establishing an O((H / epsilon)^2 log(kT / delta)) sample complexity for learning the optimal alpha.

Section 4.3.4 ('Empirical Evaluation') evaluating PTRR_alpha across alpha in {0.1, ..., 1.0} on OpenML-CC18 learning-curve instances from LCDB 1.1 (k = 22 models, T = 44 anchors), demonstrating that the optimal alpha varies significantly across datasets.

Section 4.4 ('Achieving Best-of-both-worlds Best Arm Identification') motivating best-of-both-worlds best-arm identification (BAI) in IMAB and providing counterexamples showing that prior BAI algorithms (such as UCB-style envelope methods) incur Omega(k) worst-case approximation ratios while PTRR alone fails exact BAI on benign instances.

Section 4.4.1 ('Hybrid Algorithm Family') and Definition 4.4.1 defining the two-stage algorithm family Hybrid_{alpha,B} (Algorithm 5), which runs UCB-style terminal envelope elimination up to switch time B and falls back to PTRR_alpha for the remaining horizon if no arm dominates.

Section 4.4.2 ('Best-of-Both-Worlds BAI guarantees') defining the Gap Clearance Condition GCC(B) (Definition 4.4.2) and proving that Hybrid_{alpha,B} identifies the exact best arm on instances satisfying GCC(B) while guaranteeing an Omega(k^{-alpha/(1+alpha)} f*(T)) expected terminal reward in the worst case.

Section 4.4.3 ('Sample Complexity for Tuning Curvature and Switch Parameters') bounding the number of piecewise-constant regions of the dual loss for Hybrid_{alpha,B} over (alpha, B) in (0, 1] x [T] and proving polynomial sample complexity for jointly learning the optimal curvature and switch parameters from data.

Section 4.5 ('Conclusion') summarizing Chapter 4's data-driven algorithm design guarantees for PTRR_alpha and Hybrid_{alpha,B} and outlining future directions including stochastic and restless improving bandit variants, followed by the Part II ('Social Epistemology') and Chapter 5 divider headings.
Chapter 5 opening ('Why Algorithmic Approaches?') introducing the thesis's perspective on applying theoretical computer science and algorithmic modeling to problems in social epistemology.
Heading-only block containing the subsection number '5.1.1' under 'On The Use of Models', with the essay body starting in the next block.

Section 5.1.1 ('Introduction') reflecting on the role of problem formulation and abstraction in theoretical computer science and engaging philosophy-of-science literature on how simplified mathematical models illuminate complex real-world social phenomena.

Section 5.1.2 ('Taxonomy of TCS-based Social Models') proposing a three-level taxonomy of epistemic purposes for theoretical social models—reproducing an observed phenomenon, explaining why it occurs, and suggesting an intervention—illustrated through Schelling's segregation model.

Section 5.1.3 ('Reproduce Phenomenon') analyzing the first epistemic tier of social modeling—showing that a phenomenon can arise from specified assumptions and initial conditions—and discussing verification, unintended empirical predictions, and robustness across parameter variations.

Section 5.1.4 ('Explain Phenomenon') analyzing the second epistemic tier—positing a modular causal or structural explanation for why a phenomenon occurs—and examining how competing theoretical explanations can be compared and tested.

Section 5.1.5 ('Suggest Intervention') analyzing the third epistemic tier—using a model's mechanism to design and evaluate real-world interventions—and discussing how to interpret positive or negative outcomes when deploying idealized interventions.

Section 5.1.6 ('What Models Can and Cannot Do') discussing the epistemic strengths and inherent limitations of idealized mathematical models in social domains, drawing on Potochnik's account of idealization in science.

Section 5.1.7 ('On Process') outlining a seven-step methodological process for computer scientists developing theoretical models of social phenomena, from grounding in domain scholarship and isolating abstractions to proving guarantees and validating assumptions.

Section 5.2 ('Modeling Ambition') introducing the substantive social epistemology questions studied in Chapters 6 and 7—how social evidence and behavioral traits like grit shape ambitious decision-making under uncertainty, inspired by Jennifer Morton's philosophical work.

Section 6.1 ('Introduction') introducing Chapter 6 on pessimism traps—a social epistemological phenomenon formalized by Morton [Mor22] in which members of marginalized communities rationally choose moderate goals over ambitious ones after observing predecessors fail—and proposing information-cascade models and subsidy interventions.

Section 6.1.1 ('Our Contributions') summarizing Chapter 6's contributions: modeling pessimism traps as incorrect information cascades in a single-dimensional sequential decision model, designing a temporary time-varying subsidy that sustainably flips a population to the optimal cascade with finite expected cost, extending to k heterogeneous groups with unknown optimal actions, and validating via simulations.

Section 6.1.2 ('Related Work') surveying prior literature on pessimism traps ([Mor22]), statistical discrimination and affirmative action ([CL93]), and sequential herding and information cascades ([BHW92], [Ban92], [AH97]).

Section 6.2 ('Preliminaries and Basic Model') outlining the two sequential decision-making settings studied in Chapter 6: a single sequence of T agents choosing between actions A and B, and k parallel group sequences whose optimal actions differ by group.

Section 6.2.1 ('Single Sequence Model') formalizing the Bayesian sequential decision model where each agent t observes private signal s_t with accuracy p > 1/2 and public action history H_{t-1}, deriving the posterior update (Equation 6.1), and characterizing up and down cascades via a biased random walk on the action count difference.

Section 6.2.2 ('On Our Modeling Choices') justifying the use of the information cascade framework to capture Morton's pessimism traps and discussing simplifying assumptions, such as binary actions and homogeneous payoffs.

Section 6.3 ('Time-Varying Subsidy') presenting Algorithm 6 and proving Theorems 6.3.1 and 6.3.2: a time-varying subsidy r_t proportional to the posterior odds ratio incentivizes agents in an incorrect B-cascade to follow their private signals, shifting the community into a self-sustaining A-cascade in expected 4/(2p - 1) steps and bounded expected total cost.

Section 6.4 ('Extension to multiple groups') relaxing the assumptions that all agents share the same optimal action and that the planner knows which action is optimal, considering k groups with unknown group-specific optimal actions and signal strengths.

Section 6.4.1 ('Formally Defining The Setting') and Definitions 6.4.1–6.4.2 defining the k-group sequential decision model and a randomized subsidy scheme that samples subsidy levels uniformly from a discrete grid V of candidate posterior-balancing values.

Section 6.4.2 ('Main Result') stating and proving Theorem 6.4.1 and Lemmas 6.4.1–6.4.3, which bound the number of steps T needed for the randomized grid subsidy to shift all k groups into their respective correct cascades with probability at least 1 - delta.
Section 6.5 ('Experiments') introducing the simulation study evaluating the effectiveness, cost, and scalability of the time-varying financial subsidy in breaking pessimism traps for a single group.

Section 6.5.1 ('Data Generation and Procedure') describing the simulation setup across population sizes N in {10, 100, 1000} and private signal strengths p in [0.51, 0.99], averaged over 100 trials per (N, p) pair.

Section 6.5.2 ('Results') reporting simulation results (Figures 6.1–6.4) showing that time-varying subsidies raise the proportion of correct cascades to nearly 100% across signal strengths while total subsidy cost remains bounded and independent of population size N once the cascade flips.

Section 6.5.3 ('Discussion and Implications') discussing the policy implications of the simulation findings, highlighting that temporary targeted subsidies can permanently reverse pessimism traps with decreasing per-capita cost in larger populations.

Section 6.6 ('Discussion and Conclusion') concluding Chapter 6 by connecting the pessimism-trap model and subsidy intervention back to Chapter 5's three-tier modeling taxonomy (reproducing, explaining, and intervening) and transitioning to Chapter 7.
Heading-only block containing the section number '7.1' under Chapter 7 ('A Theoretical Model for Grit'), with the introduction text following in the next block.

Section 7.1 ('Introduction') introducing Chapter 7's study of grit as a behavioral trait in ambitious decision-making under uncertainty, building on Morton and Paul's [MP19] philosophical account of grit, epistemic norms, and material scarcity.

Section 7.1.1 ('Our Approach To Studying Grit') outlining two formal models of rational decision-making for studying grit: a worst-case competitive-ratio model (where grit is parameterized via optimism about the reward slope and discomfort tolerance) and a forward-looking Bayesian model (where grit is parameterized via uncertainty tolerance).

Section 7.1.2 ('Our Contributions') summarizing Chapter 7's main findings: formalizing grit and financial safety nets in a two-armed improving bandit instance, characterizing optimal switching times and discomfort constraints under competitive-ratio rationality, comparing the benefits of a trust fund versus grit, and analyzing uncertainty tolerance in the Bayesian setting.

Section 7.1.3 ('Related Work') outlining the structure of Chapter 7 and summarizing Morton and Paul's [MP19] philosophical framework on grit, the Evidential Threshold, and how ecological and financial constraints shape rational perseverance.

Section 7.2 ('Formal Setting: Improving MAB') defining the two-armed improving bandit instance (Equation 7.1) used to model grit: a stable arm f_1 yielding constant reward 1 and a striving arm f_2 yielding 0 until an unknown threshold theta and growing linearly with slope alpha thereafter.
Heading-only block containing the subsection number '7.3.1' under 'Rationality in Terms of Competitive Ratio', with the prose body in the following block.

Section 7.3.1 ('Rationality in This Model') characterizing competitive-ratio-optimal deterministic policies in the two-armed grit bandit instance (Lemma 7.3.1), showing that any non-interleaving policy explores the striving arm f_2 for s steps before switching permanently to f_1 if no payoff is observed.

Section 7.3.2 ('Modelling Grit: Optimism') modeling grit as an agent's optimistic belief alpha_tilde about the striving arm's post-threshold growth rate alpha, deriving the competitive-ratio-optimal give-up time s = T - sqrt(2T / alpha_tilde) (Lemma 7.3.2), and analyzing how miscalibrated optimism affects achieved reward.

Section 7.3.3 ('Modelling Grit: Discomfort Tolerance') introducing a per-step striving cost (f_2(t) = -gamma before threshold theta) and a cumulative reward floor, proving in Lemmas 7.3.3 and 7.3.4 that agents without a safety net must interleave the stable arm f_1 with f_2 and thus spend less actual time exploring the striving arm.

Section 7.4 ('Financial Support') introducing external financial support (such as a safety net or trust fund) into the costly striving bandit model to compare its effect on exploration duration and reward against increasing an agent's personal grit.

Section 7.4.1 ('No Safety Net') calculating the effective striving exploration time (T - sqrt(2T))/2 for an agent without financial support who must alternate between the stable arm f_1 and the costly striving arm f_2 to maintain non-negative cumulative reward.

Section 7.4.2 ('Free Reimbursement') analyzing a safety-net model in which a benefactor reimburses striving costs whenever net reward would drop below zero, allowing the agent to explore f_2 continuously for T - sqrt(2T) steps—twice as long as an unsupported agent with the same discomfort tolerance.

Section 7.4.3 ('Which Wins? Trust Fund or Grit?') comparing the effects of higher optimism (grit) versus free-reimbursement financial support, showing that while grit increases exploration by trading off worst-case fallback reward, a financial safety net doubles exploration time without sacrificing fallback security.

Conclusion of Section 7.4.3 (titled 'Setting' from a table/header split) presenting a summary table comparing exploration time and fallback stable reward across grit levels (alpha_tilde_1 vs. alpha_tilde_2 > alpha_tilde_1) with and without a financial safety net.

Section 7.5 ('Rationality as Being Bayesian') introducing the second model of rationality in Chapter 7, where a forward-looking Bayesian agent maximizes expected reward under a prior distribution over when the striving arm begins paying off.

Sections 7.5.1–7.5.2 ('Rationality in This Model') deriving the posterior expected reward of continuing on the striving arm versus switching to the stable arm under a prior D on the threshold theta, and modeling grit as uncertainty tolerance via the prior standard deviation sigma.

Section 7.5.3 ('Results for Modelling Grit as Uncertainty Tolerance') evaluating the optimal give-up time s under a Gaussian prior N(mu, sigma^2) on theta (Figure 7.2), showing that higher uncertainty tolerance (larger sigma) causes the Bayesian agent to persevere longer past the expected payoff time mu.

Section 7.6 ('Discussion of Modelling Choices') examining how Chapter 7's two-armed bandit models map onto Chapter 5's modeling taxonomy, comparing the competitive-ratio and Bayesian formulations of grit, and noting limitations and future extensions.
Section 7.7 ('Conclusion') summarizing Chapter 7's quantitative two-armed improving bandit models of grit, optimism, discomfort tolerance, and financial support.

Section 7.8 ('Discussion in Relation to Pessimism Traps') synthesizing the insights of Chapters 6 and 7 on how social evidence (pessimism traps) and individual behavioral traits plus material resources (grit and safety nets) jointly shape ambitious decision-making.

Chapter 8 ('Conclusion') opening Part III by reviewing how the dissertation's technical results on improving multi-armed bandits and social epistemology fit together within the thesis's unifying decision-making framework.

Section 8.1 ('Interplay between sequential and social decision-making') reflecting on how the sequential decision-making perspective of Part I and the social modeling perspective of Part II complement each other when studying settings where policies and environments interact.

Section 8.2 ('General vs Specific') tracing the spectrum of abstraction across Chapters 3, 4, 6, and 7—from worst-case IMAB to distributional learning and concrete social models—to evaluate what is gained and lost at each level of specificity.
Section 8.3 ('Open Problems and Future Directions') introducing the survey of concrete technical open problems and broader research directions emerging from the dissertation.

Section 8.3.1 ('Concrete Technical Questions') listing open technical problems for improving multi-armed bandits (closing the log k gap for unknown f*(T), alternative concavity assumptions, computationally efficient ERM) and for pessimism traps and grit (more general payoff structures, continuous signal spaces, and combined social-behavioral models).

Section 8.3.2 ('Broad Future Directions') discussing broader research directions enabled by the thesis's unifying framework, including studying institution-level resource allocation, behavioral biases, and human-AI collaboration.

Section 8.4 ('Parting Thoughts') offering concluding reflections on the role of computer science in studying human and institutional decision-making, followed by the complete dissertation bibliography (pages 114–125) and the Appendix A header.

Appendix A.1 ('Proof of Lemma 3.4.4') providing the complete proof that the doubling-trick procedure in Algorithm 3 achieves expected cumulative reward at least OPT_T / (8192 * sqrt(k) log(128k)) when T > 4k is unknown.

Appendix A.2 ('Maximum Reward Objective') introducing the variant of the improving multi-armed bandits problem where the objective is to maximize the single largest reward pull rather than cumulative reward.

Continuation of Appendix A.2 (titled 'Upper Bound') noting that the main paper's cumulative-reward approximation guarantees carry over up to constant factors to the maximum-reward objective via diminishing returns.

Appendices A.2.1 and A.2.2 ('Lower Bound' and 'Upper Bound') proving the Omega(sqrt(k)) lower bound and the O(sqrt(k)) and O(sqrt(k) log k) upper bounds for the maximum-reward objective in improving multi-armed bandits.
Heading-only block containing the appendix subsection number 'A.3.1' under 'Extension to noisy rewards', with the analysis following in the next block.

Appendix A.3.1 ('Extension of Algorithm 1') proving that when observed rewards are multiplicatively noisy within [(1 - epsilon)f_i(t_i), (1 + epsilon)f_i(t_i)], a modified threshold in Algorithm 1 preserves the O(sqrt(k)) competitive ratio up to a ((1 - epsilon)/(1 + epsilon))^2 factor.

Appendix A.3.2 ('Extension of Algorithm 2') adapting the exploration bounds [m_hat_L, m_hat_U] of Algorithm 2 to multiplicatively noisy rewards within 1 +- epsilon, followed by the Appendix B title page.
Appendix B.1 ('Additional Related Work') beginning the extended literature review for Chapter 4 by summarizing foundational work on improving/rising bandits ([HKR16], [PNGK23], [BR25]).

Continuation of Appendix B.1 (titled 'Upper Bound') reviewing related work on deterministic rested rising bandits ([MTPR22], [MMT+24]), best-of-both-worlds bandit algorithms, and data-driven algorithm design ([Bal20], [SS25]).

Appendix B.2 and B.2.1 ('Full Proofs for Sharper Competitive Ratio') stating the Concavity Envelope Exponent properties and proving Theorem 4.3.1, showing that PTRR_alpha achieves an O(k^gamma) competitive ratio for gamma = max{alpha/(1+alpha), beta_I - alpha(1 - beta_I)}.

Appendix B.2.2 ('Lower Bound') constructing a hard family of improving bandit instances with concavity exponent beta_I = beta and applying Yao's principle to prove that no randomized algorithm can achieve a competitive ratio better than Omega(k^{beta/(beta+1)}).

Appendix B.2.3 ('Doubling Trick for Unknown T') proving that combining PTRR_alpha with the exploration phase and doubling trick of [BR25] removes the need to know m and T while preserving the O(k^gamma log k) competitive ratio.
Appendix B.3 ('Details for Sample Complexity Analysis') introducing the appendix section containing background definitions and full sample complexity proofs for tuning alpha in PTRR_alpha.

Appendix B.3.1 ('Results from Prior Work') restating Definition B.3.1 (derandomized dual complexity) and the uniform convergence theorem of [SS25] used to bound sample complexity in the Hyperparameter Transfer Setting.

Appendix B.3.2 ('Uniform Convergence Implies Population Loss Near-Optimality') and Lemma B.3.2 proving the standard result that uniform convergence of empirical loss over a parameter space implies near-optimal population loss for the empirical risk minimizer alpha_hat.
Appendix B.3.3 ('Average Regret') and Definition B.3.2 instantiating the H-bounded loss framework for average cumulative regret in bounded-reward improving multi-armed bandits.

Appendix B.3.4 ('Computational Complexity of ERM') proving Lemma 4.3.3 on the piecewise monotonicity and O(k! kT) critical points of the derandomized dual loss of PTRR_alpha and analyzing an exact empirical risk minimization algorithm.

Appendix B.3.5 ('An Algorithm for Finding a Suitable Value of the Parameter') proposing and analyzing a computationally efficient quantile-based algorithm for selecting a parameter alpha for PTRR_alpha from sampled instances without enumerating all k! arm permutations.

Appendix B.3.6 ('Full Empirical Evaluation') detailing the experimental setup, LCDB 1.1 dataset preprocessing, concavity verification, and full sensitivity plots (Figures B.1 and B.2) for PTRR_alpha on OpenML-CC18 benchmarks.

Appendix B.4 ('Best-of-both-worlds for Maximizing Cumulative Reward') introducing a data-driven approach to achieving sublinear policy regret on benign instances while falling back to optimal competitive ratio on general instances for the cumulative reward objective.

Appendix B.4.1 ('Motivating Examples') presenting explicit improving bandit instances where PTRR_1 incurs linear regret Omega(T) while UCB-style algorithms incur an Omega(k) competitive ratio on cumulative reward.

Appendix B.4.2 ('Data-driven Hybrid Approach') describing a parameterized family that interpolates between a rising-bandit regret minimizer and PTRR_alpha and bounding the sample complexity of learning its switching parameter over an instance distribution.

Appendix B.5 and B.5.1 ('BAI Comparison with Prior Work and Proof Details') comparing the Gap Clearance Condition GCC(B) of Section 4.4 with the fast-convergence conditions for best-arm identification in [MMT+24].

Appendix B.5.2 ('Difficulty in Corralling Improving Bandit Algorithms') proving that a standard corralling meta-algorithm that switches once from an optimistic rising-bandit algorithm to PTRR cannot simultaneously achieve sublinear regret on benign instances and worst-case competitive ratio guarantees.

Appendix B.5.3 ('Proofs for results in Section 4.4.2') proving Lemma B.5.3 (validity of the terminal envelope bounds L_i(t) <= f_i(T) <= U_i(t)) and the full best-of-both-worlds BAI theorem for Hybrid_{alpha,B}.

Appendix B.5.4 ('Proof of Lemma 4.4.2') proving that for any fixed augmented instance, the loss of Hybrid_{alpha,B} across (alpha, B) partitions into at most k T^2 piecewise-monotonic regions, bounding the sample complexity of tuning both parameters.

Appendix B.5.5 ('Cumulative Reward Best Arm Identification') defining the Cumulative Hybrid_{alpha,B} algorithm family (Algorithm 7), which adapts the two-stage envelope-then-PTRR design to identify the arm with the highest cumulative reward.

Appendix B.5.6 ('Best-of-Both-Worlds Best arm identification guarantees') defining the cumulative Gap Clearance Condition and proving that Cumulative Hybrid_{alpha,B} achieves exact cumulative-reward BAI on benign instances and an Omega(k^{-alpha/(1+alpha)} OPT_T) expected reward guarantee in the worst case.
Heading-only block containing the section number 'C.1' at the start of Appendix C ('Appendices for Pessimism Traps'), with the text following in the next block.
Appendix C.1 ('Key features of pessimism traps') summarizing the core epistemic features of Morton's [Mor22] account of pessimism traps in educational and career choices.

Appendix C.2 ('Related Works') providing an extended survey of related work across information cascades, network structures, statistical discrimination, affirmative action, behavioral economics, and social epistemology.

Appendix C.3 ('Proof for Posterior Update (Eqn. 6.1)') deriving the Bayesian posterior probability P[E_A | s_t, H_bar_{t-1}] under conditional independence of private signals and uniform prior over actions A and B.

Appendix C.4 ('Formulation as a Random Walk') proving Lemmas C.4.1–C.4.4, which characterize the sequential decision process as a random walk on the net action difference |A| - |B| with absorbing barriers at +2 and -2 and compute absorption probabilities and expected steps.
Heading-only block containing the appendix subsection number 'C.5.1' under 'Time-Varying Subsidy Proofs', with the proof of Theorem 6.3.1 in the next block.

Appendix C.5.1 ('Proof of Theorem 6.3.1') deriving the exact time-varying subsidy threshold r_t that makes an agent's expected utility for action A exceed action B iff their private signal favors A, breaking an incorrect B-cascade.

Appendix C.5.2 ('Proof of Theorem 6.3.2') applying Wald's identity to the biased random walk under the subsidy to bound the expected duration E[N] = 4/(2p - 1) and expected total cost R * 4/(2p - 1) required to reach a self-sustaining A-cascade.
Heading-only block containing the appendix subsection number 'C.6.1' under 'Details for extension to multiple groups', with the formal details in the following block.

Appendix C.6.1 ('Defining The Setting') stating and proving Fact C.6.1, which establishes the existence of a signal-revealing subsidy value v_{x,p} for any group with signal accuracy p and action imbalance x = |A| - |B|.

Appendix C.6.2 ('Analyzing the Subsidy Scheme') providing the full proofs of Lemmas 6.4.1–6.4.3 and Theorem 6.4.1 via random-walk hitting-time and Chernoff bounds for the k-group randomized subsidy scheme.
Appendix C.7 ('Extra Experiments') introducing the supplementary simulation figures for Chapter 6.
Heading-only block containing the appendix subsection number 'C.7.2' under 'Proportion Correct Cascades', with the figure captions in the next block.

Appendix C.7.2 ('Subsidy Size') containing the captions for Figures C.1–C.4 showing proportion of correct cascades and average subsidy progression over rounds for N = 10 and N = 1000 agents, followed by the Appendix D header.

Appendix D.1 ('Related Work') surveying empirical and philosophical literature on grit ([Duckworth], [MP19], [Credé]) alongside computer science work on behavioral biases (Kleinberg-Oren-Raghavan) and structured bandits.

Appendix D.3.1 ('Proof of Lemma 7.3.2') deriving the competitive-ratio-optimal switching step s = T - sqrt(2T / alpha_tilde) by equating the worst-case ratios when the striving arm never increases versus when it increases immediately after the switch.

Appendix D.3.2 ('Proof of Lemma 7.3.3') proving via an exchange argument that under a per-step striving cost and zero-floor constraint, any strategy is dominated by a minimally accumulating strategy that alternates f_1 and f_2 in a fixed ratio until switching permanently to f_1.

Appendix D.3.3 ('Proof of Lemma 7.3.4') computing the competitive-ratio-optimal switching point and effective exploration time on the costly striving arm for an agent with discomfort tolerance constraint and cost parameter gamma.

Appendix D.4 ('Fixed Time Financial Support') analyzing a bounded financial support model where a benefactor reimburses at most R steps of striving cost, deriving the resulting exploration time as a function of R.

Appendix D.5 ('Calculations For Interplay of Grit and Trust Fund') deriving the optimal switching point and exploration time when an agent with optimistic slope belief alpha_tilde faces striving cost gamma = 1 both without a safety net and with free reimbursement.
